name: Lactose intolerance
definition: Digestive symptoms such as bloating, diarrhoea and gas that follow eating or drinking foods that contain lactose, the sugar in milk.
overview: Lactose intolerance means having digestive symptoms after eating or drinking foods that contain lactose. It is linked to the small intestine not making enough lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose. The NHS says it can start at any age. It is a different condition from a milk allergy. The NHS also says most adults with lactose intolerance do not need a severely restricted or lactose-free diet.
causes: Not producing enough lactase, the enzyme that digests lactose
Bowel conditions, infections or injuries affecting the gut
Lactase production falling after infancy (lactase nonpersistence), which can cause lactose intolerance in adulthood
Another health condition, such as coeliac disease, in some people
riskFactors: Family and genetic background, with lactase nonpersistence more common in some groups, including people of East Asian descent
A recent diarrhoeal illness, which can trigger temporary lactose intolerance
signs: Symptoms that follow foods containing lactose, found by asking about symptoms and eating habits
Symptoms that improve when lactose is removed from the diet and return when it is put back
complications: Lower calcium and vitamin D intake if all milk and dairy are cut out
Confusion with other conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, which can cause similar symptoms
diagnosis: A doctor usually asks about symptoms, family and medical history and eating habits, and may examine the person and arrange tests to confirm lactose intolerance or rule out other problems. The NHS says a GP may suggest a lactose elimination diet or a hydrogen breath test. MedlinePlus describes breath, blood and stool tests, with the hydrogen breath test the most commonly used.
treatment: Most people can manage symptoms by eating less lactose or avoiding it. Taking a lactase supplement before food or drink that contains lactose may reduce or prevent symptoms for some people. The British Dietetic Association advises replacing dairy with lactose-free milk products or fortified plant-based alternatives. NIDDK recommends talking with a doctor or dietitian about dietary changes.
prevention: MedlinePlus says there is no known way to prevent lactose intolerance, although symptoms can be avoided by avoiding foods that contain lactose.
seekCare: A routine GP appointment is the usual route if symptoms keep coming back, particularly after eating, or if there is persistent bloating, blood in the stool or unexplained weight loss. Anyone who thinks a child is lactose intolerant is advised by the NHS to see a GP before removing dairy from the diet. The NHS says to call 999 for sudden confusion, dizziness, fainting or a limp, unresponsive child.

sections.heading: What is lactose intolerance?
sections.body:
Lactose is the sugar found in milk and dairy foods. Lactose intolerance means digestive trouble, such as bloating, diarrhoea and gas, after eating or drinking foods that contain it. The underlying problem is lactose malabsorption, where the small intestine produces too little lactase, the enzyme that breaks lactose down. The NHS says lactose intolerance can start at any age.

It is a different condition from a milk allergy. Tolerance varies, and NIDDK says research suggests many people can handle some lactose with no or only mild symptoms. Lactose also appears in some packaged and prepared foods, and NIDDK says a small amount may be found in some prescription and over-the-counter medicines. MedlinePlus says eating less food with lactose, or using pills or drops that help digest lactose, usually helps.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of lactose intolerance?
sections.body:
Common symptoms listed by the NHS include stomach pain or discomfort, bloating, gas, rumbling in the stomach, diarrhoea or constipation, and nausea or vomiting. NIDDK says symptoms typically start within a few hours of eating lactose. MedlinePlus says they usually appear roughly half an hour to two hours after dairy, and tend to be worse with larger amounts.

Because these symptoms are digestive and fairly general, other conditions can cause similar problems. MedlinePlus notes that irritable bowel syndrome can produce similar symptoms. A review of the evidence also notes that self-reported intolerance often does not match test results, so symptoms alone can mislead. The NHS advises seeing a GP if symptoms keep coming back, especially after eating.

sections.heading: What causes lactose intolerance?
sections.body:
The NHS says causes include not producing enough lactase, and bowel conditions, infections or injuries. In adults it can result from lactase nonpersistence, meaning lactase production is reduced after infancy. NIDDK says genes can be the reason in some cases, and that injury to the small intestine can also cause it, which is called secondary lactose intolerance. Babies born too early sometimes have lactose intolerance, according to MedlinePlus Genetics.

MedlinePlus says it is more common among adults of Asian, African or Native American heritage. In some people another health condition, such as coeliac disease, is the cause, according to NHS 111 Wales. Secondary intolerance, often following a gut infection, is mainly temporary, according to an NHS clinical guidance page. MedlinePlus says that when a short diarrhoeal illness was the trigger, lactase levels typically recover within a few weeks.

sections.heading: How is lactose intolerance diagnosed?
sections.body:
A doctor usually asks about symptoms, family and medical history and eating habits. The doctor may also carry out a physical examination and tests to confirm lactose intolerance or to rule out other problems. The NHS says a GP may suggest a lactose elimination diet, in which lactose is removed from the diet and then put back to see whether symptoms return.

The other approach the NHS describes is a hydrogen breath test, which measures hydrogen in the breath to see how well lactose is digested. MedlinePlus says the lactose-hydrogen breath test is the most commonly used test. It also describes a lactose tolerance blood test, which looks for a rise in blood glucose after a lactose drink. MedlinePlus adds that a doctor may use a blood, breath or stool test to find out whether problems are due to lactose intolerance.

sections.heading: How is lactose intolerance managed day to day?
sections.body:
Most people can manage symptoms by eating less lactose or avoiding it, according to the NHS. The NHS also says most adults with lactose intolerance do not need a severely restricted or lactose-free diet. Taking a lactase supplement before food or drink that contains lactose may reduce or prevent symptoms for some people. The British Dietetic Association advises replacing dairy with lactose-free milk products or fortified plant-based alternatives.

NIDDK says managing symptoms usually means adjusting intake rather than cutting out dairy entirely. It warns that cutting out all milk and dairy can reduce calcium and vitamin D intake, and recommends talking with a doctor or dietitian about changes. MedlinePlus says milk is a major source of calcium, so a person who does not get enough from the diet may need a calcium supplement. MedlinePlus adds that symptoms can be avoided by avoiding foods that contain lactose, and that there is no known way to prevent the condition itself.

faqs.q: Is lactose intolerance the same as a milk allergy?
faqs.a: No, NIDDK describes lactose intolerance as a different condition from a milk allergy. Lactose intolerance is linked to the small intestine making too little lactase, and it causes digestive symptoms such as bloating, diarrhoea and gas. Anyone unsure which applies is advised by the NHS to see a GP if symptoms keep coming back.

faqs.q: Do people with lactose intolerance have to avoid all dairy?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, as the NHS says most adults with lactose intolerance do not need a severely restricted or lactose-free diet. NIDDK says many people do not need to avoid all foods that contain lactose, and that cutting out all milk and dairy can reduce calcium and vitamin D intake. A doctor or dietitian can advise on changes.

It depends on the cause. When it follows a short diarrhoeal illness, MedlinePlus says lactase levels typically recover within a few weeks. NHS clinical guidance describes secondary intolerance, often after a gut infection, as mainly temporary. Where lactase production falls after infancy, MedlinePlus Genetics describes it as a reduction in lactase production.

faqs.q: How do doctors test for lactose intolerance?
faqs.a: The NHS says a GP may suggest a lactose elimination diet or a hydrogen breath test. The breath test measures hydrogen in the breath to see how well lactose is digested. MedlinePlus also describes a lactose tolerance blood test, which looks for a rise in blood glucose after a lactose drink, and says stool tests may be used.

The NHS says taking a lactase supplement before having food or drink that contains lactose may reduce or prevent symptoms for some people. MedlinePlus says pills or drops that help digest lactose usually help, together with eating less lactose. A doctor or dietitian can advise on whether they suit a particular person.
